turns.line: Okay, so it's four filters in a row. Why not just build one really steep filter?
turns.speaker: student

turns.line: Because steepness from a single stage would need exotic parts and would be a nightmare to control. Four gentle, identical stages is elegant — and each transistor rung gives you a handle for voltage control for free.
turns.speaker: teacher

turns.line: And resonance is just… echoing the output back into itself?
turns.speaker: student

turns.line: In phase, yes. The frequencies near the cutoff arrive back just in time to reinforce themselves. It's like pushing a kid on a swing — tiny pushes at the right moment build into something huge.
turns.speaker: teacher

turns.line: So self-oscillation is the swing going over the top?
turns.speaker: student

turns.line: Exactly. At maximum resonance the loop sustains itself with no input. You've turned a filter into an oscillator — which is why early synth players tuned the filter cutoff like a second instrument.
turns.speaker: teacher

plan.hook: One clever arrangement of transistors gave every Moog its growl — and taught a generation what electricity sounds like when it sings.

questions.explain: Each rung contributes 6 dB/octave, so 12 dB/octave means two stages. A single RC stage is 6 dB/octave; the classic Moog ladder is 24.
questions.q: A 12 dB/octave filter is best described as…

choices: The capacitors are matched by hand
Each transistor stage's corner frequency shifts with the same control current
questions.explain: The control current sets the operating point of every transistor rung simultaneously, so all four corners move in lockstep. Matched parts help, but the mechanism is the shared control current.
questions.q: Why can one control voltage sweep all four stages together?

choices: Boosts frequencies near the cutoff, and can cause self-oscillation at max
questions.explain: Resonance is in-phase feedback that peaks the response at cutoff. Cutoff, distortion character, and slope are separate matters.
questions.q: Turning up resonance on a ladder filter…

sections.body:
A single resistor-capacitor stage is a gentle slope: past its corner frequency it shaves off **6 dB per octave** — halving the signal each octave up. Moog's insight was to stack four of these stages in series, like rungs of a ladder, each buffered by a transistor so one stage can't drag down the next.

Four rungs × 6 dB = **24 dB per octave**. That's a cliff, not a slope. Below cutoff your bass sails through untouched; an octave above, it's 24 dB down — roughly a sixteenth of the voltage. That steep wall is the Moog sound's foundation: it lets a bright, buzzy sawtooth keep its body while the harsh top gets cleanly removed.

The transistors do double duty. They buffer the stages, and — because a transistor's behavior shifts with current — they make the cutoff **voltage-controllable**. One control voltage climbs the whole ladder at once, sweeping all four corner frequencies in lockstep. That's why the filter tracks the keyboard: the cutoff follows your playing.
sections.heading: Four rungs make a ladder

questions.answer: Without buffering, each RC stage would load the previous one, shifting its corner frequency and ruining the neat 6 dB-per-stage math.
questions.hint: Think about what happens when you connect two RC filters directly…
questions.q: Why does the ladder need buffering transistors between stages?

questions.answer: 800 Hz is two octaves above cutoff, so about 48 dB down — essentially gone.
questions.hint: Count the octaves above cutoff, multiply by 24.
questions.q: A sawtooth at 100 Hz goes through the filter with cutoff at 200 Hz. Roughly how much quieter is the 800 Hz harmonic?

sections.body:
Take some of the filter's output and feed it back to the input, in phase, and something magical happens: frequencies *near the cutoff* get amplified instead of cut. Turn the resonance knob and a peak grows at the cutoff point — the sound gets nasal, vocal, hollow. Push it further and the peak becomes a spike.

At maximum, the feedback is strong enough that the circuit **oscillates on its own** — it produces a pure sine wave at the cutoff frequency with no input at all. The filter has become an instrument. Wendy Carlos used this singing quality to make the filter weep and scream on *Switched-On Bach*.

Like a hockey slapshot, it's all about the feedback loop: energy returned at just the right moment builds instead of dying away. Too little and nothing happens; too much and it takes off on its own.
sections.heading: Resonance: feeding the output back

questions.answer: A sine wave at the cutoff frequency — self-oscillation.
questions.hint: The feedback loop no longer needs an input to sustain itself.
questions.q: What does the filter output when resonance is maxed and there's no input?

bullets: Control current sweeps all corners together
sections.notes: Start with the single RC stage — everyone knows a tone knob. Then the trick: stack four, but buffer them so the math stays clean. Four times six is twenty-four, and that steep wall is the whole Moog sound. The kicker: one control voltage moves every rung at once.

sections.notes: Resonance is just feedback with manners. A little gives you that vocal wah; a lot gives you a whistle with no input at all. Carlos made a career out of that whistle.
